A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ConceptPrism. Their complete main texts and appendices are readable, and corresponding methods, equations, tables, and figures can be reliably matched despite reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original DreamBench evaluations, training-time measurements, ablations, GPT-4o assessments, and qualitative personalization experiments, including FLUX examples.

after.justification: v2 retains these original results and adds initialization controls, reference-diversity tests, comparative FLUX evaluations, and multi-concept generation examples.

M1.justification: The core token optimization, reconstruction and exclusion losses, and subsequent LoRA fine-tuning remain unchanged, including Algorithms 1–2. v2 adds a multi-concept inference adaptation: independently learned concepts are combined through LoRA merging and multiple target tokens, without joint training.

E1.justification: v2 adds subject-subject and subject-style composition tasks and a reference-set scenario testing shared background confounding. Existing dataset coverage and single-concept FLUX demonstrations are retained; explicitly naming CustomConcept101 in the main text does not introduce a new dataset.

E2.justification: v1's FLUX evidence demonstrates only ConceptPrism. v2 substantially expands this comparison scope by evaluating SynCD and OminiControl, labeled OminiCtrl in Tables 7–8, through quality scores, qualitative examples, and runtime comparisons. The original DreamBench and abstract-style comparator sets remain unchanged.

E3.justification: v2 introduces frozen-residual and shorter-caption control conditions, multi-concept composition settings, and comparative FLUX quality and runtime evaluations; the new timing experiment specifies an H100 GPU. Original DreamBench sample totals, metrics, preprocessing, training budgets, and inference settings remain unchanged. The PDFs do not establish that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New Table 4 tests dependence on caption length and residual-token optimization by comparing frozen, short, medium, and long initializations. New Figure 7 examines unintended shared backgrounds and a counterexample intervention. These targeted analyses supplement the retained component, token-length, exclusion-weight, and residual-token analyses.

E5.justification: Table 1 retains its four-seed statement and identical plus-or-minus reporting. The residual-token visualization still uses three seeds. The added experiments introduce no new repeated-run information, uncertainty-estimation procedure, confidence intervals, or significance testing.

E6.justification: Original benchmark, ablation, and GPT-4o scores are retained, but v2 adds substantial comparative and diagnostic results. Table 7 reports CLIP-T/DINO of 0.362/0.213 for ConceptPrism, 0.300/0.269 for SynCD, and 0.346/0.174 for OminiCtrl: ConceptPrism leads CLIP-T but trails SynCD on DINO. Table 8 adds runtime results, Table 4 adds initialization-control scores, and Figures 7 and 11 add robustness and composition outcomes. These are newly reported conditions, not demonstrated performance gains over v1.

T1.justification: The mathematical objectives and supplementary Gaussian-KL-to-noise-matching derivation remain unchanged. Revised explanatory prose and section numbering introduce no new assumptions, formal results, or proofs.

C1.justification: v2 omits v1's explicit claim to be the first method using inter-image comparison for personalized concept disentanglement, retaining a more general novelty claim. The central claims about automatic disentanglement, complementary losses, and improved fidelity-alignment trade-offs remain.

C2.justification: v2 explicitly acknowledges that unintended features shared across references can be learned as part of the target, and discusses counterexamples as mitigation. It also attributes gains to token optimization rather than caption quality and explains the training-cost versus inference-speed trade-off against encoder-based methods. These add substantive qualifications and interpretations.

D1.justification: v2 identifies an H100 for the new FLUX timing experiment and describes independent concept training followed by LoRA merging. However, it removes v1's FLUX-specific bfloat16, 8-bit AdamW, and 512-by-512 resolution disclosures. Core Stable Diffusion settings, algorithms, and Gemini caption-generation instructions remain.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including B-LoRA, Tokenverse, SynCD, OminiControl, ZipLoRA, and SSR-Encoder, and discusses recent DiT-based personalization. The encoder-based versus optimization-based taxonomy and positioning against externally guided disentanglement remain substantially intact.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, method explanations, and experimental discussion undergo extensive rewriting. Related work moves from Section 6 to Section 2, evaluation metrics are consolidated into experimental setup, and supplementary comparisons and additional applications are separated into distinct sections.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual presentation with initialization Table 4, FLUX Tables 7–8, reference-diversity Figure 7, comparator Figure 10, and composition Figure 11. Existing diagrams and result images are retained, while appendix galleries are reordered or resized and main-table captions and placements are revised.

improvement.justification: The initialization controls and explicit shared-background failure case improve scrutiny of the mechanism and its applicability boundaries. FLUX comparisons provide useful evidence beyond v1's standalone examples, and the rewritten structure improves exposition. These are incremental gains over an already substantial evaluation. Sparse documentation of the new FLUX comparisons and removal of earlier implementation details limit the reproducibility benefit, but do not outweigh the added diagnostic evidence.
